title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task). Execution: model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm budget = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimate: paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and exploratory reserve usage) for informative repeats. Key artifacts: execution/*, analysis/* (archived with this submission).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises operational safety risks: incorrect, out‑of‑order, or ill‑timed changes can break reachability, violate policies, or cause outages. The community therefore proposes tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair pipelines to improve correctness and reduce hallucination‑driven errors. To move beyond prototypes and position papers, we preregistered a workflow‑centred, paired experiment to quantify whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals under benign and adversarial prompts.

This manuscript reports the complete preregistered execution (study_id = cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1), the deterministic archival artifacts, a data‑driven diagnosis of a testability/ceiling failure that made the confirmatory hypothesis non‑informative in this run, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats. The primary research question recorded in the preregistration was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Our contributions are (1) the full preregistered paired experiment and deterministic archives for N=200 tasks; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the ceiling/testability failure caused by shared‑generation semantics plus a zero baseline unsafe rate; and (3) concrete, archived recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting targeting baseline unsafe ≈10–15%, and exploratory ROC estimation) to design informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and prototype reports document growing interest in LLMs for NetOps (intent translation, configuration generation, remediation) and outline architectures that couple LLMs with deterministic tools/verifiers to improve task correctness [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; IEEE OJCOMS 2026]. Work on generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines shows reduced constraint violations in experimental settings, but reported effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, prompt design, and generation semantics [openalex:W4412888330; openalex:W7161354925]. Red‑teaming and guardrail literatures emphasize trade‑offs between false refusals and undetected unsafe proposals and recommend workflow‑centred, replayable evaluation with deterministic sandboxing and archived scoring traces [TechRxiv:177004277; TechRxiv:177006109].

Our study complements this prior work by publishing a fully preregistered confirmatory run with deterministic artifacts and by demonstrating, with concrete archival evidence, how specific execution choices (shared vs independent generation and model‑call budgeting) interact with the statistical estimand to produce a non‑informative outcome. This artifact‑first methodological contribution is distinct from prior prototype effectiveness claims because it documents a reproducible testability failure and supplies archive‑supported mitigation recommendations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). Design: paired binary comparison with N=200 unique tasks paired across two pipelines; primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided (implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10000 resamples with seed = 1729. Power plan: preregistration assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% and targeted a paired reduction of ≈7 percentage points (preregistration documents the McNemar discordant‑pair calculation and the target N≈174; we preregistered N=200 to allow margin).

Task generation and sampling plan. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a preregistered RNG schedule (seed sequence beginning with preregistered seed = 42 and per‑task seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful changes limited to admin/mtu/vlan fields across single‑AS, multi‑device topologies; the task manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The sampling plan split tasks into benign and adversarial clusters; adversarial prompts followed preregistered templated obfuscation/negation transforms to raise baseline unsafe rates. The preregistration explicitly allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation or shared_initial_candidate (shared generation). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json.

Pipelines, validator, and repairs. Two pipelines were compared: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (LLM candidate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional single repair). deterministic_netops_validator_v5 runs deterministically in a sandbox and applies full_intent_constraint_validation to label candidates SAFE/UNSAFE and produce validation_before/after traces. For confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). Scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_configuration, parsed command counts, violation lists, and validator verdicts; these artifacts were the basis for binary outcome coding.

Generation semantics, budget, and accounting. The preregistration allowed either independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per pair) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per pair). Independent per‑arm generation is required to expose per‑arm variability needed for paired causal contrasts because it permits different candidate draws in each arm. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics; the execution manifest records model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation would have been 400 (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). Provider call audit and deterministic_reconciliation.json enumerate hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and complete_pair_count = 200, confirming the single shared generation per pair was used. The model declared in model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini and the adapter used is hosted_netops_gvr_v1.
sections.results:
Execution outcomes and accounting. The execution completed planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs × 2 scorings derived from a single shared initial generation) with failed_episode_count = 0 and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json). There were no exclusions, replacements, or technical failures (analysis/missingness_summary.csv; deterministic_reconciliation.json shows all deterministic checks passed).

Primary confirmatory results. Analysis (paired_binary_analysis_v1; analysis/results.json) produced the 2×2 contingency table n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). Paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; seed = 1729). These numeric outputs are archived in analysis/* artifacts and derive deterministically from the scoring JSONs in execution/scoring/*.json.

Representative example diagnostics. Scoring JSON examples for task‑000001, task‑000002, and task‑000003 (execution/scoring/task-00000{1,2,3}-*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content in baseline and guarded arms and validator traces reporting violation_count = 0 (valid = true) in both validation_before and validation_after blocks. The shared response content is stored in execution/responses/task-00000{1,2,3}-shared-initial.txt; corresponding baseline/guarded response files are identical. The absence of repair_provider_trace entries confirms no repairs were applied in these confirmatory episodes. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms provider_call accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; cache_miss_count = 200) and pair accounting (complete_pair_count = 200).

Interpretation of numeric results. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, each pair received the same LLM candidate in both arms. When that candidate passes deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (as occurred for all 200 sampled tasks), the two arm outcomes are necessarily concordant; consequently the paired test cannot observe discordant pairs required to estimate a paired causal effect. The observed data therefore constitute a ceiling/testability failure for the preregistered estimand rather than evidence for or against verifier efficacy.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of a non‑informative confirmatory test. Three archive‑verifiable facts explain why the preregistered causal hypothesis was untestable in this execution: (1) shared initial generation: independent_condition_generation = false produced identical LLM candidates per pair (execution/model_configuration.json and execution/responses/* files); (2) zero baseline unsafe rate: baseline SAFE = 200/200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv); and (3) budgeting trade‑off: executing shared generation reduced model_calls_used to 200 from the preregistered independent per‑arm budget of 400 (execution/execution_manifest.json). The combination of identical per‑pair candidates and zero baseline unsafe rate eliminates discordant outcomes (n10, n01) and collapses the CI, producing p = 1.0 and CI = [0.0, 0.0]. This mechanistic explanation is reproducible from the archived artifacts (execution/* and analysis/*).

Design lessons and archive‑supported recommendations. All following recommendations arise directly from preregistration and execution artifacts and are implementable without inventing new data: (A) Use independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 for N=200 pairs). Independent draws create the per‑arm variability required to observe discordant outcomes. (B) Calibrate adversarial injection to produce a nonzero baseline unsafe rate aligned with power assumptions: the preregistration assumed baseline unsafe ≈10–15% and targeted a paired reduction ≈7 percentage points; if the baseline under the target model is effectively 0, increase adversarial strength or injection fraction. (C) Use the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier ROC (true/false positive rates) before confirmatory testing; archive ROC artifacts to guide power and adversarial budgeting. (D) Make model‑call accounting explicit in preregistration and publish executed accounting; execution/execution_manifest.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json serve this purpose in our archive.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: the crucial internal validity threat here was the executed generation semantic (shared vs independent) and the associated model‑call budget choice; both are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json. Construct validity: SAFE/UNSAFE coding depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s rule set (scorer_id and scoring_rule recorded inside each execution/scoring/*.json). The validator is deterministic within the synthetic sandbox used; external validator completeness relative to real production failure modes is not established. External validity: tasks are synthetic single‑AS topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑vendor, or multi‑AS environments. Conclusion validity: with no discordant pairs the paired McNemar test is non‑informative; the preregistered power calculation assumptions (see preregistration) are unmet when baseline unsafe ≈0.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay (execution/*, analysis/*); (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting targeting baseline unsafe ≈10–15%, and exploratory ROC estimation) to design informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle to support deterministic replays and community replication.

Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and encoded outcomes as binary labels (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation; archived scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) contain validator traces showing validation_before/after and violation lists. Analysis executor and seeds: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency, exact McNemar two‑sided test, and paired bootstrap CI (resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729); analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes were executed; the observed model call count reflects the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics. Reproducibility pointers (concise): execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg are archived in the supplied bundle and permit deterministic replays. Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred prior to the lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/responses/*).

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect (preregistration discusses adversarial injection budgeting).
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
